occurrenceRemarks: Convict Surgeonfish (Acanthurus triostegus) are a common reef-associated species found throughout the tropical Indo-Pacific region. These fish are easily recognizable by their pale white to grayish body marked with five to six bold vertical black stripes, giving them the appearance of a traditional prison uniform hence the name “convict.” They have an oval, laterally compressed body and a small mouth with comb-like teeth, adapted for grazing. Primarily herbivorous, convict surgeonfish feed on benthic algae and play an important ecological role in controlling algal growth on coral reefs. They are typically found in shallow lagoons and reef flats and often form large, active schools. At Pasikuda Beach, Sri Lanka, convict surgeonfish are frequently observed in nearshore reef areas. Local small-scale fishermen occasionally report catching them as bycatch, indicating their abundance and interaction with coastal fisheries in the area.

identificationRemarks: I sent this link to John Pogonoski, who forwarded it to Huang Wen-Chien. Here's what he had to say: "This record shows a typical Strophidon sathete. Among the four uniformly brown species of the genus, S. sathete and S. ui have similarly slender bodies as shown in the photo, but S. ui does not reach this size and has not been recorded in the Indian Ocean. Additionally, S. tetraporus usually has a much lighter body color with black-edged fins, whereas S. sathete is generally dark brown throughout."
occurrenceRemarks: This was discarded from a fisherman's net on the beach while fishermen were going through their catch. It was at least 7' long for certain, possibly over 8' long. They said it came from 2.5km offshore. Later in the night I came around again, and began to stretch it out to measure it when I realized it was still alive I drug it into the surf and pushed it head-first through the water to force air through the gills. The eel took a second to get mobile but eventually swam off with normal-looking movements.

identificationRemarks: The Red Sea, Gulf of Aden, and Gulf of Oman populations of *M flavolineatus* were named as the separate subspecies *M flavolineatus flavicaudus* by [Fernandez-Silva et al. in 2016](https://zookeys.pensoft.net/article/8060/). This was done largely because these populations all have a yellow tail fin, in contrast to the gray tail fin mostly found elsewhere. There is also a difference in eye size. In 2018 Golani and Fricke elevated the subspecies to the full species *Mulloidichthys flavicaudus* in their [2018 checklist of Red Sea fish](https://www.mapress.com/zt/issue/view/zootaxa.4509.1), although with no discussion. And Catalog of Fishes (of which Ronald Fricke is a curator) now treats it as a full species. When I asked Ronald Fricke about this (in regard to another fish) he explained that it was done because Catalog of Fishes doesn't recognize subspecies. Since iNaturalist regards Catalog of Fishes as the ultimate authority in fish taxonomy, this observation should probably be changed to *Mulloidichthys flavicaudus*. The species is listed as legitimate in iNat, but has no observations as of this post, Sept 2, 2025! @francoislibert
